info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 9.1: Manual Entity Identification, Authority Record Research, and Canonical Citation.

name.text: 01 Question: Names Beyond Strings: Why Editions Need Entity Markup

questiontext.text: Why is plain-text string searching inadequate for identifying historical entities in a digital scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: Entity markup connects variant historical names to stable real-world entities, overcoming the ambiguities of literal text strings.

answer.text: A single historical entity can appear under multiple spelling variants, aliases, and titles, while identical strings can refer to completely different entities.

feedback.text: Correct. Plain strings cannot distinguish between different people sharing a name or gather variant historical spellings together without semantic entity markup.

answer.text: Plain-text search algorithms are illegal under international copyright and manuscript preservation treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Copyright law does not prohibit string searching in digital humanities software.

answer.text: Modern web browsers refuse to display documents that do not contain semantic XML markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers display plain text easily; entity markup serves research and semantic linking.

answer.text: Text search engines require supercomputers and cannot run on archival documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. String searching is computationally simple and fast, but semantically blind.

name.text: 02 Question: The Four Core Classes: People, Places, Organizations, and Dates

questiontext.text: What are the four primary entity classes standardized in digital humanities research?

generalfeedback.text: Digital entity markup models historical records through four core classes: persons, places, organizations, and dates.

answer.text: Persons, Places, Organizations, and Dates.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital humanities and computational linguistics focus on these four foundational categories to map historical actors, geography, institutions, and chronologies.

answer.text: Fonts, Margins, Bookbindings, and Paper Sizes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are physical and typographic layout features, not semantic named entities.

answer.text: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs, and Conjunctions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are grammatical parts of speech, not named entity classes.

answer.text: Manuscripts, Microfilms, Hard Drives, and Flash Drives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are physical and digital storage media, not entity classes.

name.text: 03 Question: TEI P5 Chapter 13: The Four Core Elements

questiontext.text: Which set of XML elements from TEI P5 Chapter 13 encodes the four core entity classes?

generalfeedback.text: TEI Chapter 13 provides specialized elements: , , , and for tagging named entities in text.

answer.text: <persName>, <placeName>, <orgName>, and <date>

feedback.text: Correct. TEI P5 Chapter 13 defines for people, for places, for institutions, and for chronological points.

answer.text: <person>, <place>, <organization>, and <calendar>

feedback.text: Incorrect. and describe entity definitions in the header, while , , , and tag inline mentions in body text.

answer.text: <name type="person">, <location>, <corp>, and <time>

feedback.text: Incorrect. While generic exists, Chapter 13 standardizes specialized tags , , and .

answer.text: <who>, <where>, <group>, and <when>

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are not standard TEI P5 tags for named entities.

name.text: 04 Question: Names with Internal Parts: Surnames, Forenames, and Titles

questiontext.text: How does TEI allow editors to break down complex personal names into structured subcomponents?

generalfeedback.text: Subcomponents like , , and provide granular structure within parent tags.

answer.text: By nesting , , , or inside a parent element.

feedback.text: Correct. Naming subcomponents like forenames, surnames, and titles can be granularly tagged inside .

answer.text: By separating the names with semicolons and storing them in an external CSV spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI embeds structured subcomponents hierarchically within XML elements.

answer.text: By converting the entire personal name into capital letters and removing all vowels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI preserves historical spellings and casing rather than modifying the surface text.

answer.text: By restricting personal names to exactly two words per individual.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI places no arbitrary word count limits on personal names.

name.text: 05 Question: Places with Layers: Towns, Counties, and Countries

questiontext.text: Which TEI child elements allow editors to capture hierarchical geographic information inside ?

generalfeedback.text: Hierarchical places are cleanly modeled in TEI using , , , and inside .

answer.text: <settlement>, <district>, <region>, and <country>

feedback.text: Correct. TEI provides geographic hierarchy elements like (town/city), (county), (province/state), and .

answer.text: <street>, <postalCode>, <apartmentNumber>, and <floor>

feedback.text: Incorrect. While postal address elements exist in TEI for modern mail, historical geography uses settlement, district, region, and country.

answer.text: <latitude>, <longitude>, <altitude>, and <satellite>

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coordinates are recorded using , not XML element wrappers around text tokens.

answer.text: <forest>, <river>, <mountain>, and <valley>

feedback.text: Incorrect. Specific landforms use or feature typing rather than standard administrative hierarchy tags.

name.text: 06 Question: Time on the Page: The Essential @when Attribute

questiontext.text: Why is the @when attribute essential when tagging historical dates with the element?

generalfeedback.text: The @when attribute supplies machine-readable ISO 8601 dates (YYYY-MM-DD) for historical temporal expressions.

answer.text: It normalizes ambiguous, non-standard, or archaic scribal phrasing into machine-readable ISO 8601 standard dates (YYYY-MM-DD).

feedback.text: Correct. The @when attribute records the normalized date (e.g. @when="1791-08-25") while preserving the original historical text inside the element.

answer.text: It forces web browsers to reload the web page at a specific time of day.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The @when attribute is an analytical data attribute, not a browser timer.

answer.text: It deletes the scribe's original historical wording from the digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI preserves the historical surface text inside the element unchanged.

answer.text: It calculates the exact monetary cost of transcribing the historical document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The @when attribute handles temporal data normalization, not project finances.

name.text: 07 Question: When Capital Letters Lie: Scribes and Common Nouns

questiontext.text: Why can an editor not rely solely on capitalization to identify proper named entities in eighteenth-century texts?

generalfeedback.text: Capitalization in early modern documents reflects rhetorical emphasis and stylistic convention, not named entity status.

answer.text: Eighteenth-century scribes and printers frequently capitalized common nouns for emphasis, while some lowercase words are proper names.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical orthography routinely capitalized ordinary nouns like 'Treaty', 'Peace', or 'Gold', so capitalization does not guarantee a proper entity.

answer.text: Eighteenth-century printing presses did not possess capital letter blocks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Movable type printing presses included full uppercase type cases.

answer.text: Scribes only capitalized words when writing in secret diplomatic code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Capitalization of common nouns was standard orthographic convention in eighteenth-century English.

answer.text: Capital letters were wiped from manuscripts during modern museum conservation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conservation stabilizes paper and ink; it does not erase letter casing.

name.text: 08 Question: Why Text Strings Fail: Connecting Names to Real Things

questiontext.text: What fundamental problem arises when two historical individuals in a corpus share the exact same name string?

generalfeedback.text: Disambiguating identical name strings requires linking them to unique entity records rather than matching raw text.

answer.text: String identity causes polysemy or entity confusion, merging two distinct historical biographies into a single query result.

feedback.text: Correct. Two people with the same name string must be disambiguated through unique entity identifiers to prevent conflation.

answer.text: The operating system halts and throws a memory allocation error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers have no problem storing identical text strings.

answer.text: The XML parser automatically deletes one of the two names from the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers do not delete content due to shared names.

answer.text: Both individuals are automatically merged into a single person in real historical records.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The people remain historically distinct; failure to disambiguate is an editorial error.

name.text: 09 Question: Three Global Registries: Wikidata, VIAF, and GeoNames

questiontext.text: What are the primary target domains for Wikidata, VIAF, and GeoNames respectively?

generalfeedback.text: Wikidata, VIAF, and GeoNames serve as foundational global registries for linked open entity data.

answer.text: Wikidata covers structured general entities, VIAF aggregates library authority records for persons/orgs, and GeoNames standardizes global geographical places.

feedback.text: Correct. Wikidata provides structured semantic web items (Q-numbers), VIAF unites international library authorities, and GeoNames identifies spatial places.

answer.text: Wikidata registers medical patents, VIAF indexes legal deeds, and GeoNames lists real estate prices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These registries are open scholarly authorities for general knowledge, library catalogues, and geography.

answer.text: Wikidata tracks computer hardware, VIAF monitors internet routers, and GeoNames stores astronomy star maps.

feedback.text: Incorrect. None of these registries are computer hardware or astronomy registries.

answer.text: Wikidata, VIAF, and GeoNames are identical copies of Wikipedia with no structural differences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each registry has a distinct architecture, identifier schema, and authority scope.

name.text: 10 Question: The TEI @ref Attribute: Building the Linked Data Bridge

questiontext.text: How does an editor connect a TEI entity element to an external authority file like Wikidata or GeoNames?

generalfeedback.text: The @ref attribute bridges TEI elements to global Linked Open Data registries through canonical URIs.

answer.text: By placing the canonical Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) or prefixed identifier in the @ref attribute of the entity element.

feedback.text: Correct. The @ref attribute stores canonical URIs (e.g. @ref="https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q38" or @ref="wikidata:Q38").

answer.text: By typing a footnote at the very bottom of the printed page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Footnotes provide human prose, whereas @ref creates machine-actionable Linked Data.

answer.text: By embedding an executable Python script inside the XML text node.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML documents do not execute inline Python scripts inside text nodes.

answer.text: By creating a new internet domain name for every historical person.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors link to existing authority registries via established URIs.

name.text: 11 Question: Local and Regional Registers: Canadian and Indigenous Databases

questiontext.text: Why must editors of Canadian historical documents consult national and regional registries like the Dictionary of Canadian Biography (DCB) alongside global databases?

generalfeedback.text: Regional databases like DCB, Native Land Digital, and local archives provide critical depth missing from global registries.

answer.text: Global registries like Wikidata have systemic representation gaps regarding regional Canadian historical figures and Indigenous leadership.

feedback.text: Correct. Regional and specialized repositories contain rich biographical and historical evidence omitted from broad global databases.

answer.text: Canadian law forbids referencing non-Canadian databases in university publications.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no legal restriction against using international databases.

answer.text: International databases like Wikidata charge high licensing fees for Canadian users.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikidata and VIAF are free and open-access public resources.

answer.text: Canadian historical figures were legally forbidden from having international records.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many prominent figures appear internationally, but regional figures are often omitted.

name.text: 12 Question: The Verified Absence Rule: When a Person Has No Record

questiontext.text: Under our course editorial rules, what must an editor do when a historical person cannot be found in Wikidata, VIAF, or regional authority files?

generalfeedback.text: The Verified Absence rule requires explicit documentation and local ID minting when no external record exists.

answer.text: Document a Verified Absence by citing the searched registries, recording search dates, and creating a local project identifier.

feedback.text: Correct. If an exhaustive search reveals no record, editors document the verified absence and mint a local URI (e.g. #person-001) rather than guessing.

answer.text: Invent a plausible-sounding fictional URI and pretend the record exists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inventing fake URIs corrupts scholarly linked open data integrity.

answer.text: Delete the person from the historical transcript to maintain database compliance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never alter or delete historical witnesses to satisfy database requirements.

answer.text: Halt the entire digital edition project permanently until an external record appears.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly workflows document verified absences locally and proceed.

name.text: 15 Question: Case Study 1: Political Entities in Ace's 1791 French Decree

questiontext.text: In Ace's 1791 French Revolutionary decree, which entity class best categorizes the 'Comité des décrets'?

generalfeedback.text: Institutional governing bodies like the Comité des décrets are encoded as .

answer.text: <orgName>, because it represents an official governmental committee and institutional body.

feedback.text: Correct. Legislative committees, clubs, and corporate assemblies are tagged as organizations ().

answer.text: <persName>, because it is composed of individual human beings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The committee is a collective institution, not an individual person.

answer.text: <placeName>, because the committee met in a physical building in Paris.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The meeting place is geographic, but the committee itself is an organization.

answer.text: <date>, because the decree was approved in August 1791.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree date is temporal, but the committee is an institution.

name.text: 16 Question: The National Assembly and the King: Royal and Legislative Bodies

questiontext.text: How did political authority in France split in the August 1791 constitutional decree?

generalfeedback.text: The 1791 decree reflects constitutional monarchy: legislative authority in the National Assembly and royal executive authority in Louis XVI.

answer.text: Between the legislative power of the elected National Assembly and the executive royal authority of King Louis XVI.

feedback.text: Correct. The 1791 Constitution established a constitutional monarchy dividing power between the legislative assembly and the crown.

answer.text: Between the Pope in Rome and the Ottoman Sultan in Istanbul.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The 1791 French decree was an internal French constitutional reorganization.

answer.text: Between private commercial shipping corporations and labor guilds.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree concerns national state sovereignty, not commercial guilds.

answer.text: Between local parish priests and rural municipal mayors exclusively.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The National Assembly and the monarch held constitutional sovereignty.

name.text: 17 Question: French Authority Files: Using BnF and IdRef for Revolutionary Names

questiontext.text: Which French national databases provide the most authoritative Linked Data records for eighteenth-century French figures?

generalfeedback.text: BnF and IdRef provide the primary canonical authority registries for French historical persons and institutions.

answer.text: Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF) and IdRef (Identifiants et Référentiels pour l'enseignement supérieur).

feedback.text: Correct. BnF and IdRef are France's national bibliographic and higher education authority registries, offering detailed French historical biographical records.

answer.text: The British Royal Navy Admiralty Registry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The British Admiralty does not maintain French domestic political authority files.

answer.text: The United States Library of Congress Copyright Office.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The LC records American copyrights and is not the primary authority for French revolutionary officials.

answer.text: The International Olympic Committee Historical Database.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The IOC records modern athletic competitions, not French revolutionary history.

name.text: 18 Question: Case Study 2: Personal Names in Olyvia's 1967 Maud Lewis Letter

questiontext.text: Why do personal letters like Maud Lewis's 1967 correspondence present unique challenges for named entity identification?

generalfeedback.text: Epistolary texts present informal names, first-name mentions, and private local networks requiring local prosopography.

answer.text: Letters feature informal nicknames, first names without surnames, and references to local neighbors not recorded in global encyclopedias.

feedback.text: Correct. Epistolary writing relies on intimate, informal naming that requires careful historical contextualization.

answer.text: Letters are written in secret invisible ink that cannot be digitized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical correspondence is written in standard ink on paper.

answer.text: Letters never mention real people or geographic locations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Letters are rich in personal names, family relations, and geographic settings.

answer.text: TEI guidelines explicitly forbid encoding private correspondence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI has extensive guidance specifically for epistolary and correspondence markup.

name.text: 19 Question: First Names and Nicknames: Resolving 'Everett' in Letters

questiontext.text: When Maud Lewis writes 'Everett' without a last name, how should an editor resolve this entity?

generalfeedback.text: Contextual knowledge resolves informal first-name mentions to full historical identities via @ref attributes.

answer.text: Tag the mention with and link via @ref to the authority record for Everett Lewis (or a local project identifier).

feedback.text: Correct. Contextual historical knowledge identifies Everett as Maud's husband Everett Lewis, allowing linked disambiguation.

answer.text: Alter the manuscript text by forcibly inserting 'Lewis' into Maud's handwritten sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never silently alter historical surface text; markup supplies external identity.

answer.text: Refuse to tag the word because it lacks an explicit surname.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Valid entities should be tagged even when expressed informally.

answer.text: Assume 'Everett' refers to the city of Everett, Massachusetts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Archival biographical context clearly identifies Everett Lewis, not a distant city.

name.text: 20 Question: Maritime Places: Marshalltown, Digby, and Nova Scotia

questiontext.text: How do the geographic entities in Maud Lewis's letters reflect spatial hierarchy?

generalfeedback.text: Geographical hierarchy cleanly nests local hamlets (Marshalltown) inside counties (Digby) and regions (Nova Scotia).

answer.text: Marshalltown is a settlement within Digby County, which is situated within the province of Nova Scotia.

feedback.text: Correct. Spatial nested hierarchy places the local settlement within its municipal district and provincial region.

answer.text: Digby is a sovereign nation containing Canada and North America.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digby is a town and county in Nova Scotia, Canada.

answer.text: Marshalltown, Digby, and Nova Scotia are identical synonymous names for the same street.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They represent three distinct levels of geographic scale.

answer.text: Nova Scotia is a small house located inside Marshalltown.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nova Scotia is the Canadian Atlantic province containing Marshalltown.

name.text: 21 Question: Case Study 3: Sovereign Entities in Andromeda's 1752 Treaty

questiontext.text: Which sovereign nations entered into the 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: The 1752 Treaty engaged sovereign Mi'kmaw leadership and the British colonial crown in mutual diplomatic relations.

answer.text: The Mi'kmaq Nation (represented by Chief Sachem Jean-Baptiste Cope) and the British Crown (represented by Governor Hopson).

feedback.text: Correct. The 1752 Treaty represents a bilateral diplomatic agreement between the Mi'kmaw nation and the British colonial sovereign.

answer.text: The Kingdom of Spain and the Republic of Venice.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither Spain nor Venice was party to Nova Scotia peace and friendship treaties.

answer.text: The Hudson's Bay Company and the Russian Empire.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty was concluded between local British colonial authorities and the Mi'kmaq.

answer.text: The United States of America and the Dominion of Canada.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In 1752, neither Canada nor the United States existed as independent federal states.

name.text: 22 Question: Mi'kmaw Leadership: Chief Sachem Jean-Baptiste Cope

questiontext.text: How should Chief Sachem Jean-Baptiste Cope's title and personal name be encoded in TEI?

generalfeedback.text: Structured personal names combine for diplomatic titles with and within .

answer.text: <persName><roleName>Chief Sachem</roleName> <forename>Jean-Baptiste</forename> <surname>Cope</surname></persName>

feedback.text: Correct. Tagging Cope with structured roleName, forename, and surname honors both diplomatic title and personal identity.

answer.text: <title>Chief Sachem</title><name>Jean-Baptiste Cope</name>

feedback.text: Incorrect. denotes creative or published works; diplomatic and political titles belong in <roleName>.</p>

answer.text: <placeName>Jean-Baptiste Cope</placeName>

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cope is a revered historical human leader, not a geographic place.

answer.text: <orgName>Jean-Baptiste Cope</orgName>

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cope is an individual human actor, not an impersonal organization.

name.text: 23 Question: Colonial Government: Governor Peregrine Thomas Hopson

questiontext.text: In the 1752 Treaty, what role does Peregrine Thomas Hopson occupy, and how is his authority grounded?

generalfeedback.text: Governor Peregrine Thomas Hopson signed the 1752 Treaty under the authority of King George II.

answer.text: Governor-in-Chief of Nova Scotia, representing the sovereign authority of King George II of Great Britain.

answer.text: A private French merchant trading furs without government sanction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hopson was the official British royal governor.

answer.text: An anonymous clerk with no political authority or signature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hopson signed and sealed the treaty as Governor-in-Chief.

answer.text: A Spanish naval admiral stationed in the Mediterranean Sea.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hopson was British governor stationed in Halifax, Nova Scotia.

name.text: 24 Question: Historical Toponyms: Chigabenakady and Colonial Renaming

questiontext.text: Why is the historical place name 'Chigabenakady' significant when editing the 1752 Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Historical toponyms like Chigabenakady reflect authentic Indigenous geography (Sipekne'katik) that predates colonial renaming.

answer.text: It represents the ancestral Mi'kmaw toponym for Sipekne'katik (anglicized as Shubenacadie), preserving Indigenous geographic heritage before colonial distortion.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical editions record indigenous toponyms to preserve authentic place names obscured by later colonial mapping.

answer.text: It was a fictional mythical kingdom invented by British poets in London.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Chigabenakady is an authentic historical Mi'kmaw regional location.

answer.text: It is the Latin translation of the city of Paris, France.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is an indigenous Mi'kmaw placename in Nova Scotia.

answer.text: It was a printing typographical error with no real-world meaning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The toponym refers to the ancestral Shubenacadie river region.

name.text: 25 Question: Regnal Years and Calendars: The King's Reign in Dates

questiontext.text: What is a regnal date in eighteenth-century British official legal documents?

generalfeedback.text: Regnal years express legal dates by counting the elapsed years of a monarch's reign alongside the Julian or Gregorian calendar.

answer.text: A date calculated from the anniversary of a monarch's ascension to the throne (e.g. 'the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King George the Second').

feedback.text: Correct. Regnal dating measures legal time relative to the reigning king's coronation year.

answer.text: A date determined by the position of Jupiter's moons through a telescope.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Astronomical planetary tables were not used for legal regnal dating.

answer.text: A secret calendar only understood by tax collectors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regnal dating was standard public legal notation throughout the British Empire.

answer.text: A date that changes every day according to the weather.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regnal years were mathematically fixed by royal accession dates.

name.text: 26 Question: Writing Your Editorial Policy: ENTITY_POLICIES.md

questiontext.text: Why must a digital edition project compile a formal ENTITY_POLICIES.md document before starting entity annotation?

generalfeedback.text: ENTITY_POLICIES.md locks in editorial rules for entity spans, classification edge cases, and authority linking.

answer.text: To establish explicit, repeatable decision rules for entity boundaries, ambiguous mentions, missing records, and canonical registries.

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial policy documents ensure consistency, prevent subjective drift, and document methodological constraints.

answer.text: Because computer operating systems refuse to run Python scripts without a markdown file in the folder.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software execution does not depend on project policy markdown files.

answer.text: To register the project with international patent offices for commercial profit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly digital editions are academic research projects, not commercial patents.

answer.text: To list the student authors' favorite movies and leisure activities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ENTITY_POLICIES.md outlines rigorous philological tagging guidelines.

name.text: 27 Question: The 20-Entity Ground Truth Table

questiontext.text: What is the methodological purpose of manually compiling a 20-entity ground truth table?

generalfeedback.text: The manual 20-entity ground truth table establishes the gold standard needed to evaluate automated models.

answer.text: It serves as the gold-standard benchmark against which automated tools (NER models and LLMs) can be rigorously scored and audited.

feedback.text: Correct. An authoritative human baseline is essential to measure precision, recall, and error rates of machine models.

answer.text: It serves as a decorative graphic to display on the university homepage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The ground truth table is an empirical scholarly benchmark.

answer.text: It fulfills a legal copyright requirement to transfer ownership of the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground truth benchmarking is an analytical evaluation method.

answer.text: It replaces the entire full text of the original historical document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The table benchmarks a curated sample excerpt, not replacing the witness.

name.text: 28 Question: Hand-Authoring ground_truth_entities_manual.xml

questiontext.text: When authoring the manual ground-truth XML fragment, how should entity tags interact with word tokens?

generalfeedback.text: Hand-authored TEI fragments must preserve full text context and maintain well-formed XML token boundaries.

answer.text: Entity tags must wrap complete word spans cleanly, respecting document hierarchy without crossing structural tags or dropping punctuation.

feedback.text: Correct. Valid XML demands well-formed nested structures with precise token boundary alignment.

answer.text: Entity tags must be inserted randomly into the middle of word syllables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Splitting syllables with entity tags creates invalid tokens and destroys searchability.

answer.text: All words that are not entities must be deleted from the XML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Full text context must be preserved for token alignment and reading.

answer.text: Entity elements must be written in uppercase HTML rather than lowercase TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI P5 elements are case-sensitive and must be written in lowercase.

name.text: 29 Question: Validating Your Entity Markup in VS Code

questiontext.text: Which tool in Visual Studio Code verifies that your TEI XML fragment conforms strictly to TEI P5 schema rules?

generalfeedback.text: Real-time TEI schema validation in VS Code catches malformed elements and invalid attributes immediately.

feedback.text: Correct. Schema validation in VS Code flags syntax errors, invalid elements, and illegal attributes in real time.

answer.text: The Windows Media Player audio equalizer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Media players play sound files; they do not validate XML schemas.

answer.text: The Microsoft Excel spreadsheet spellchecker.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Excel is a spreadsheet tool, not an XML schema validator.

answer.text: The Google Chrome cookie settings panel.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browser cookie settings manage web privacy, not TEI schema validation.

name.text: 30 Question: The Stage Gate: Committing Your Manual Entity Baseline

questiontext.text: Why is committing your manual entity files to git before running automated tools an essential scientific stage gate?

generalfeedback.text: Committing the manual baseline locks in an uncorrupted scientific gold standard before running automated algorithms.

answer.text: It guarantees an immutable, version-controlled baseline that cannot be accidentally overwritten or biased by subsequent machine predictions.

feedback.text: Correct. Version control locks in the human gold standard before exposing it to automated experiments.

answer.text: Because Git automatically rewrites and improves student code when committed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git records historical snapshots; it does not alter or improve human analysis.

answer.text: Because GitHub deletes repositories that do not commit files every two hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub does not delete repositories based on hourly commit frequencies.

answer.text: Because committing to Git instantly deploys the files to the national library.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local commits record changes in the working tree without external publication.
